why: Kahn's algorithm run backwards and layer by layer: use out-degree instead of in-degree, peel every current leaf at once, and the parents whose last child was removed form the next layer. Nodes that never peel off sit on a cycle.
hints: Kahn's algorithm removes nodes with no incoming edges. What changes if you remove nodes with no outgoing edges instead?
Track each node's out-degree and its parents. Removing a leaf decrements the out-degree of each parent.
Layer = sorted nodes with out-degree 0; emit it, then build the next layer from parents that dropped to 0 and sort it. If fewer than n nodes were emitted, return []. O((n + E) log n).
pitfalls: Emit whole layers in ascending order; do not interleave a newly freed parent with the current layer.
A cycle anywhere means the whole answer is [].
